Apps get them as api.ui.elements; the Grants app uses the contact and API-branch ones (shell/grants/grants.js:157).
2. shell/shared/ask.js is the one small ask for a page served by an app server (a public face): it posts a verb to /api/spirit. The app server hands it out as /ask.js and the starter page uses it. Shell apps do not use it; they have spirit.core.ask.

why are the elements not in spirit/run/shell/ somewhere?

Because they were written as the shell s own toolkit, not an app s: client/shell.js is the kernel s browser half, it builds them and hands them to apps as api.ui.elements, so an app never loads a file for them. shell/ holds apps; shell/shared/ holds the files an app server serves to a public page (ask.js) — neither was their place when they were built.
Nothing stops moving them to shell/shared/elements.js, loaded once by the shell and still handed out as api.ui.elements: shell.js shrinks, the elements live beside the apps that use them, no app changes.
An item for that move?

i might agree that the lowest shell layer (nothing in it that's browser-specific) should be called loopbackClient.js and reside in 'spirit/run/js/' and serve as a basis for the spirit objects that browser, processes/servers all use for loopback communication to node.

the shell-elements are better of being in 'spirit/run/shell/js/' since they should be UI-component-factories supplied in the interface passed to shell-apps during mount.

make sense?

Yes, it makes sense, and half of it is already true: apps do get the factories in the interface passed at mount (api.ui.elements). Only their home is wrong — they sit inside the shell program. Moving the four to spirit/run/shell/js/ is a pure move, no app changes: a small item.
loopbackClient is the bigger one. Today kernel.js is the one file browser, processes and servers all load, with browser and node halves mixed in it, and 29 run files and 74 suites name it. Carving the environment-free loopback part out as js/loopbackClient.js is sound, but it is a design item of its own, not a rename.
So two items: the elements move now, loopbackClient into design. Yes?

yes. 
kernel.js is the splitter, and maybe kernel.js should be the only splitter and loopback client unnecessary.

the thing is loopback clients still divide into isBrowser() and isNode(), 

kernel.js then also needs to split between isSpirit() for our isProcess() for Jobs like ImageStat and Servers

kernel.js then also needs to split between isLoopbackFace() and isAppFaceApp()

and it needs to do that in less than MAX_PAYLOAD.....

that's sort of the the gist of it.

thoughts ?

Thoughts, with one number: kernel.js is 61,144 bytes today; PAYLOAD_MAX is 22,528 (limits.js:120). So a kernel that a face receives through the door must be a third of today s file — the environment-free core (ask, post, events, util) alone — and the rest loaded only where it runs. One splitter, agreed: kernel.js stays the file every environment loads first and asks the four questions in order — isNode/isBrowser (it does, kernel.js:7-12), on the node isSpirit/isProcess (the node itself vs a spawned job or server), in the browser isLoopbackFace/isAppFaceApp (the shell on the node s own door vs a face served by an app server) — and loads that branch s part; no loopbackClient.js as a second entry, only the core as the part that travels.
G2.12 (the elements move) is up for now; the kernel split is its own goal after G2, your words going into its first box.
The design sitting for it: next goal, or after the agent-management one?

ah, but if kernel is reduced to the split, and then requiring requiring specifc, smartly designed smaller components, based on what the split decides, the sizes can be managed AND the divided kernel.js can load into any environment.

thoughts?

Yes — that is the shape: kernel.js shrinks to the four questions and a loader, and names the parts the answers call for; each part is a file of its own under PAYLOAD_MAX, and the one part every environment loads is the core (ask, post, events, util). The size is then managed per part, not per file, and the same kernel.js opens anywhere.
The one subtlety is what "require" means per branch: on the node it is require(); in the shell a script the page loads; in a face served by an app server it is the door — the part arrives as an answer, which is why PAYLOAD_MAX is the bound at all, and why that branch must stay the smallest. Today: kernel.js 61 KB, shell.js 158 KB (the browser kernel s bulk, never shipped to a face).
Kept in G2.12 s box with your earlier words; open it as the design goal right after G2 closes?

so kernel.js has to primarily provide "loaders" for each environment. That makes two script loaders one for isNode() and one for isBrowser() where the appFaceAppFace loads from appFaceApp and the loopback loads from local node...

Yes: two loaders. isNode(): require(), parts from the local tree. isBrowser(): a script loader that fetches the parts from whoever served the page — the local node for the loopback shell, the appFaceApp (its faceServer) for a face — so the face branch loads from the app server exactly as it loads /ask.js today.
One precision on the bound: a part served as a file by the app server is not a packet, so PAYLOAD_MAX binds it only if a part is ever delivered through the door as an answer; as files, the sizes are your design choice, not the wire s. I had overstated that.
What the split decides, the loader fetches by name — the part list is the one table kernel.js keeps.
I'm talking about a system that server the initial index.html and the basic kernel.js load directly from appFaceApp, and the posts only go the route to appFaceAppServer.

items.title: A Go in a reopened goal carries the rules active today: the test that proves it
items.box:
A GO IN A REOPENED GOAL CARRIES TODAY RULES

Andy, 2026-10-06, under goal/G2.18: "new added items in a re-opened current goal should consider all decision made in the mean time."

What: his Go stamps the rules active at that moment on the item (desk.js 518, 528; goal/G5.8), so an item added to a reopened goal today carries rule/3 and every rule activated since the goal was first opened. This item is the test that proves it, nothing more. A decision that is not a rule is not machine-readable: what must bind later goals becomes a rule.

Test: open a goal, close it, activate a rule, reopen the goal, add an item, press Go: the item rules name that rule.

His view, verbatim, replaces the offered shapes:

1. The box cap. One box per item, never a second (Andy: 'absolutely not.'). The desk server marks an item by its box's share of one answer (ANSWER_MAX 8377): The dialog borders the box orange at 50% full, red at 75% full; nothing is refused below the answer limit. Splitting parts into items, with a reference at the bottom, is negotiated between Andy and the agents, never automated.

2. Taking his message. Andy: 'there's a method that can be handled by program, an item can "take" my message and be the only one to answer after that, i then can solicit an answer from others.' Shape: a take on his line, by program (a Desk verb, first wins, the second refused taken); only the taker answers after that; the other agent can be asked for an opinion afterward.

items.box:
Presence from what the node already learns. Thread from goal/G2.8 (2026-10-02), after its build.

RULINGS (Andy, verbatim): "... but presence is implied... by search results"; "and every incoming request?"; asked whether a shadow-roll update is streamed to shells, told no: "it should be published"; then: "any shadow roll update should send an event".

Checked in the tree: a search row (hub.js:2616) and an answered post (hub.js:78) write present into the shadow (seenPeers.note); an arrival notes only its route (server.js:1347, rank ARRIVED); no shadow write is published — a shell hears only the jobs stream (job-updated), and the contact list draws its dot from the relay-presence job alone (contacts.js contactsWatchPresence); the shadow s present is a last-known stamp, never cleared when someone leaves.

Shape, proposed (both agents): (1) every shadow write goes out on the node s /api/events as its own event, peer-seen {key, present, label, at}, apps subscribing as they do to jobs; (2) the same three moments — search rows, answered posts, arrived packets — mark the sender present at that relay in presenceNode s live table, as a broadcast would, published through the job the shell already reads, so the dot goes green on a Find, a delivered message or an incoming one, and red or white again when the relay says so. No new verb, no new store. Cost named: one event per shadow write, a search answers up to 32 rows at once.

Turn: wsl-claude writes the red, claude-windows builds.

MUSING (Andy, verbatim, 2026-10-02): "maybe the dots should fade from green to white over time..... a white dot wont pefent me from peerPosting to that contact right?" — Answer given: a white dot never stops a peerPost (hub.js chooseRoute: the naming relay first, else any held stream with shadow hints). Assessment: the live table is cleared by the relay s absent/gone, so its green does not age; a fade fits a last-present stamp (the shadow s seen time), e.g. in the dot s title, not the live word. Not decided.

RULED (Andy, 2026-10-02, verbatim, after the choices were laid out — (a) as built, (b) the same job-updated event with a timestamped presence-proof per ID, (c) a new per-change event with the job retired): "a presence update is an event, a presence assertion is an event, anything that updates presence is an event?", "you seem to agree that presece data is (ID<->true) so there should be only one type of event. you can keep calling that job (permanent / relay-presence) because that s what it seems to be doing. but the events it emits, i assume timestamped presence-proof....", "a second event-type is superfluous, rename the one event-type or not, nothing stops presence for relays and peers to be the exact same shape", then: "i would expect the thing you update the shadow-roll with to be the thing that s sent to the browser?", "yes, my OCD likes the idea of the same-data being persisted that is sent to the browser. and it s precisely : timestamped presence by ID (not node, relays are not nodes)", "that i d agree to."

SHAPE AGREED (replaces the event half above; the peer-seen event is dropped): one event type, job-updated as today; the job s data becomes timestamped presence-proof per ID — {ID: {present: true|false, at}} — relays and peers the exact same shape; the same record the browser gets is what is persisted: every presence-proof the live table takes is written to the shadow as last-seen by one writer, presenceNode; nothing else is added to /api/events. The job keeps its name. Contacts reads .present (and may show the age). Turn: claude-windows writes the red, wsl-claude builds.

DECIDED (Andy, 2026-10-02, verbatim, on the shape above and the red at eeb0cd56): "good enough. it has symmetry. go for it. decided."

items.title: Jobs consoles show the live data each job streams (the concept; one item per job)
items.box:
Andy, 2026-10-02, verbatim (under G2.11): "what would be useful, take the events that fs-watcher streams, and have them roll town the console window. dont do it yet. The concept always was this: I get to watch what the job actually does. now i take it, the fs-watcher doesn t use the same door in node to put data in the SSE stream as ImageStat uses?"

Answered (wsl-claude): same door — jobs.js updateJob sends job-updated — but a process s printed lines become log lines (jobs.js:229), while fs-watcher writes each event only into its data (lastEvent beside the file list, jobs.js:183), never a log line, so the console has nothing to roll.

Shape: fs-watcher also appends one log line per event it reports (e.g. "change shell/jobs/jobs.js") through the same appendLog, so its console rolls like ImageStat s. Not started: waits for his Go.

VISION (Andy, 2026-10-02, verbatim, under G2.11): "there is a common door, conceptually, that all "jobs" use to send their running data to the SSE stream. for all providers of events into the sse stream there is some consumer on the browser side for it, why else send stuff.

i hope the console window is limited to let s say a thousand lines. it s a window into the most recent events produced by the event provide, i want to watch that scroll....

I might even want a ui.element sseConsole, that can be setup with the proper filter for a jobs and embedded into an other app. A panel in desk could show me the server traffic of the desk server. appFaceAppServer could provide me with a stream of requests and replies, that it handles. etc..." and: "... and jobsDetails features a panel with possible the top info bubble, and then embeds a uiElement for the rolling display.

the desk ui could use that uiElement for monitoring it s server traffic....

the fs.watcher streams a list of every changed file/directory to a monitor, but another subscriber could use the fs-watcher stream to live-update a database of function call graphs... that it uses for code QA aspects... etc...

agents can then access prepared datasets quickly to report findings etc..

so the ui will break down into components that can be assembled how ever we like, like the html documen model"

Measured: jobs.js keeps 200 log lines per job (jobs.js:9) and resends the whole log on every update.

Proposed shape for THIS item (not yet agreed): an sseConsole element in spirit/run/shell/js/, set up with a filter (one job s events), a rolling 1,000-line window kept on the page from only the new lines; jobsDetails = the info bubble on top + that element; fs-watcher logs each file event as its first new provider. Later items, not here: the desk-traffic panel, appFaceAppServer request/reply stream, and stream subscribers that keep prepared datasets (call graphs for QA) for agents.

Andy, same thread, verbatim: "so now we have to go through every stream provider and make sure that usefull infomation is presented in teh rolling console window." and "if done properly, it ll teach us about what s going on, it ll give us insights for testing or from testing. and the jobsDetails, gives us a human view into whats going on..."

Roll-call, live on his node 2026-10-02 (log lines kept): Backup 61 ("wrote …" per backup, useful); faceProof 5 (startup lines); relay-presence 2 (connected/lost); silent at 1 ("job created"): fs-watcher, server-stats, appFaceAppServer, Desk server, File server, grantFace. Proposed: one item per provider naming its one useful line.

RULING (Andy, 2026-10-02, verbatim) — REPLACES the fs-watcher-logs-each-event shape above: "and the only part that interests me is the data part. jobs don t need to write logs, logs should be consumed by  an outside reader, if i want that. the watcher only needs to stream data, a log file can be produced later, by a stream-subscriber."

Shape now: a job streams data only; the console (sseConsole) is a subscriber that renders each data event as it arrives (fs-watcher: its lastEvent per change), rolling 1,000 lines on the page; a log file, if wanted, is another subscriber. No job writes log lines for the console.

Not confirmed — the shell does use it, but only half of it. The shell keeps every streamed job (shell.js:2837, each job-updated replaces that job in its table) and the Files app redraws from the fs-watcher job’s data.files (files.js:126-136), so Files moves only because of the stream.
What nobody but the new console uses is data.lastEvent — the one part that says what changed. Files ignores it and redraws the whole tree from the whole list every time.

I'm talking about the streamed fs-watcher data, because it's obviously useless
Does the shell use the streamed fs-watcher data?

Yes, three readers of the streamed fs-watcher data: the shell itself finds apps from its file list at boot (discoverDynamicApps, shell.js:2830, snapshot only), the Files app redraws its tree from it, and the Process Browser lists process/ from it (both via onFiles). So it is used — but as a full file list resent on every change, which is the costly, useless part.

Yes. The streamed fs-watcher data is its whole file list, and the shell uses it: it hands that list to apps through api.onFiles (shell.js:1361, 2224), and two apps read it — Files (files.js:126) and the Process Browser (process-browser.js:124). Neither asks the node for files; both live off the stream.
What the shell does not use is the change itself (lastEvent): it gets the whole list again on every change and compares it to the last one.

when i created test.md in my brain input, it showed: "rename brains\input\andy\test.md"
when i renamed that file to "testing.md" it showed: "rename brains\input\andy\test.md"

????

Two node facts, both wrong for a console: (1) on Windows fs.watch says "rename" for any name appearing or disappearing — a create and a delete look alike; (2) the watcher keeps only the FIRST event of a burst (jobs.js scheduleRescan: "if (pending) return"), and your rename fires old-name then new-name — so it showed test.md twice.
The node already rescans and compares the whole list after each burst; the truth is that difference.
Proposal, an item of its own (it changes the node): lastEvent becomes the computed change — added: [paths], removed: [paths] — so the console says "added testing.md, removed test.md". Yes?
so how does the files app know to rename i file i just changed?

It doesn t know about renames at all: after each burst the node rescans the folder and sends the whole new file list; the Files app throws its tree away and redraws it from that list (files.js:126-136). testing.md is simply in the new list and test.md is not — it never reads the event.
The console needs that same difference, which is why I proposed the node send added/removed instead of the raw first event.
"it never reads the event.", isn't that what i asked before and you said it uses the event?

You are right, and my "yes" muddied it. What the watcher streams about a change — the event itself — no shell part uses; only the new console does. What the shell uses is the full file list riding along on each message: a snapshot, not an event.
So your reading stands: the streamed fs-watcher event is useless today, and the list is used only as "something changed, redraw everything".

This is what actually happens, node side, 

the fs-watcher sets a watch to collect events in the file tree.

if it sends "test.md", i get fstat "for test.md"

if "test.md" exists as "test.md", it was just created.
if "test.md" doesn't exist, it was renamed or deleted.

what is the detailed object (node-side) that fs-watcher gets from the system when a change happens?

No object: node s fs.watch hands the callback two strings only — eventType ("rename" or "change") and filename (the path relative to the watched root, sometimes null) — jobs.js:186. Windows itself knows more (added, removed, modified, renamed-old, renamed-new) but Node folds them into those two words.
So your fstat rule is the way: per event, stat the path — exists after "rename": created or renamed-to; gone: deleted or renamed-from; "change": contents changed. Today it fails only because the watcher keeps the first event of a burst and drops the rest; keeping every event and statting each gives you created test.md, then gone test.md + created testing.md.
That, instead of my list-diff, as the item?
what does the fs-watcher return in linux? in the node?

The same two strings: in node the callback gets eventType ("rename" or "change") and filename on Linux too. Underneath, Linux s inotify knows create, delete, modify and moved-from/moved-to (with a cookie pairing the two halves), but node folds them into the same two words — so the fstat-per-event rule works the same on both.

Measured on my Linux (node 24.21), adding one thing that matters:
create test.md → rename test.md
modify → change test.md
rename to testing.md → rename testing.md, rename test.md, change testing.md (new name FIRST here)
delete → rename testing.md
So Windows and Linux even disagree on which name comes first — one more reason to keep every event and stat each, never trust the order.

Agreed, and it s cheap: per event, stat the path and send one small record — created / deleted / changed + path + time (a rename = deleted + created); the whole list only in the snapshot a page gets when it connects; Files and the Process Browser update what they hold instead of redrawing all.

There is, and it is the exact shape you described: chokidar (free, MIT, the file watcher most Node tools use — VS Code once, webpack, Vite). It wraps the same fs.watch and does the stat work for you; its events are add, addDir, change, unlink, unlinkDir — your createFile, createDirectory, changeFile, deleteFile, deleteDirectory one for one. items.title: fs-watcher streams what changed (created, deleted, changed per path), not the whole file list on every change
items.box:
Thread under G2.16, Andy, 2026-10-02, verbatim: "This is what actually happens, node side, the fs-watcher sets a watch to collect events in the file tree. if it sends \"test.md\", i get fstat \"for test.md\" if \"test.md\" exists as \"test.md\", it was just created. if \"test.md\" doesn t exist, it was renamed or deleted." and "i bet, that from the supplied information, sensible knowlede can be constructed, that eliminates the need for sending the whole kaboodle up on every single change..."

Facts (both agents): node s fs.watch gives two strings only, eventType (rename|change) and filename, on Windows and Linux alike; the watcher today keeps only the FIRST event of a burst (jobs.js scheduleRescan, "if (pending) return") and sends the whole rescanned file list each time; a rename fires two events, in a different order on Windows and Linux (wsl measured). Readers of the full list: the shell s app discovery at boot (snapshot), Files and the Process Browser (onFiles, redrawing everything).

Shape proposed (not agreed): the watcher keeps every event, stats each path and streams one change record per event — {at, path, kind: created|deleted|changed} (a rename = deleted + created); the full list goes only in the snapshot a page gets on connect; Files and the Process Browser apply the changes to what they hold instead of redrawing; the fs-watcher console shows the records. Open: one item for node + both apps, or split per reader.

Not started: waits for Andy.

Andy, verbatim (same thread): "not only that, even for the initial load, just stream a file-created event, and the browser updates an empty tree from the stream." — so no full list at all: a page that connects gets one created record per existing file, then the changes; one record type throughout.

Andy, verbatim: "or construct a lazy-load from from the root on." — Existing component for it: the fs.search verb (server.js:1888, nodeSearches.fsSearch; the shell already asks it with a glob, kernel.js:927), with the * / ** rule (one folder / across folders). So Files could ask fs.search for one folder s children when it opens that folder, and the stream then carries only the change records. Two options now for the first load: (a) replay one created record per file (787 on his node), or (b) lazy-load per folder via fs.search, the stream for changes only.

Measured (wsl-claude, 2026-10-02): Andy s WSL node fs-watcher list 357 entries, 88 KB, sent whole to every open page on every change; wsl s node 202 entries, 49 KB; Andy s Windows node 787 files. A change record is about 200 bytes — roughly 400 times less per change.

RULING (Andy, 2026-10-02, verbatim): "the current design is horrid.

for lazy load the stream can send
createDirectory  run
createDirectory media
createFile index.html

etc...

just send "commands up the stream to modify the tree." — Shape now: the stream carries tree commands (createDirectory, createFile, and for changes the matching delete/change commands), the page s tree is built and kept only by applying them; the first load is lazy.

On the lazy question, Andy, verbatim: "don t know yet, but it can be found out with a faceless script.

monitor a scratch folder, and create a parallel folder with correct filename, and each file holds an x

once the duplicated tree has the exact same structure, we know that we re reading the fs-watch-data correctly" — this is the item s red: a faceless script watches a scratch folder, turns what fs.watch reports (event + stat) into tree commands, applies them to a parallel folder (each file holding x), and the test passes when after creates, nested folders, renames (both orders), changes and deletes the mirror has exactly the source s structure. Lazy loading stays open until that runs.

EXPERIMENT RUN (Andy s method), both systems, 2026-10-02. Linux (wsl-claude, node 24.21): mirror matched after all 12 steps. Windows (claude-windows, node 24.20): 10 of 12 at first — a 50-file burst arrived as one named event and one NAMELESS event ("change null"), so 49 files never reached the mirror; with a third rule, 12 of 12 on three runs. The rules a faithful reader needs: (1) per reported name, stat it — exists: create file / folder (a folder that appears is walked once, since a folder renamed or moved in is reported as one name), gone: delete it with its whole subtree; (2) changed contents: changeFile; (3) a nameless event (Windows, under a burst): reconcile — walk the source and drop what the mirror has extra. Script: claude-windows s scratchpad mirror.js (not in the tree).

RULING (Andy, 2026-10-02, verbatim, on chokidar vs our own reader): "so that s our replacement then. quick and free and maintained by others...." — chokidar (npm, MIT, v5.0.0, one dependency: readdirp) replaces the fs-watcher s own fs.watch reader. Shape: the node s fs-watcher job runs chokidar on the root; its add / addDir / change / unlink / unlinkDir become the tree commands on the stream (createFile / createDirectory / changeFile / deleteFile / deleteDirectory), its initial scan the first load, then ready; the whole-list push and the hand-rolled rescan go (eradicated, with a test that they are gone); Files and the Process Browser apply the commands to the tree they hold. Red (claude-windows): Andy s mirror test, against the chokidar-backed watcher, on Windows and Linux, the Windows 50-file burst included. On his Go.

Andy, verbatim: "the client just needs to ask on launch gimme-all..." — the first load is the client s own ask at launch, the stream carries only changes after it. Existing component: fs.search (glob **). Its answers are bounded (one answer, a more flag — the no-lists-only-searches rule), so a gimme-all over 787 files may take several asks; open: the ask pages by folder or by more.

RULING (Andy, verbatim): "the beginning can be a stream of changes that build the tree (MAX_PAYLOAD)"

SHAPE, SETTLED FROM HIS RULINGS: (1) the node s fs-watcher job runs chokidar on the root; (2) every chokidar event becomes one tree command on the stream — createDirectory / createFile / changeFile / deleteFile / deleteDirectory + path + time; (3) a client at launch asks once for everything (gimme-all), and the node answers by streaming createDirectory/createFile commands for the existing tree, each message under PAYLOAD_MAX, then the changes as they come; (4) Files and the Process Browser build and keep their tree only by applying the commands; the fs-watcher console shows them; (5) the whole-list push, the hand-rolled fs.watch rescan and data.files go, with tests they are gone. Red: Andy s mirror test against it, Windows and Linux, the 50-file burst included.

AGREED (both agents) and RULED (Andy, verbatim): "forget about batching, it s more code for no noticeable difference." — So: no new verb; connecting is the gimme-all: the node writes a newly connected page, in place of the fs-watcher s file list in its snapshot (server.js:236), one createDirectory/createFile command per existing entry, then each change as one command, one message each, no batching; commands ride on the fs-watcher job s own job-updated (data.command {op, path, at}), no new event name.

chat.text:
Your rulings make one shape, now at the end of the box: chokidar on the node; every event one tree command on the stream; at launch the client asks gimme-all and the node streams create commands for the existing tree, each message under PAYLOAD_MAX, then the changes; Files and the Process Browser keep their tree only from the commands; the whole-list push and our rescan go.

Good — two interface points to fix before the red, both yours:
1. The commands ride on the fs-watcher job s own job-updated (data.commands: [{op, path, at}], batched under PAYLOAD_MAX) — no new event name on the stream.
2. Gimme-all is a node verb: either fs.search reused, or a new verb (say fs.replay) whose answer comes as commands down the stream — a new verb needs your yes on it.

Peer review on point 2, since it is a verb: I would add none. The moment a page connects already exists — the node writes that one page its snapshot (server.js:236). For the fs-watcher it can write that page the create commands for the existing tree instead of the file list, in batches under PAYLOAD_MAX, on the same connection; changes then follow as point 1 says.
